title: Does a duty of care exist?
caption: After Robinson, start with precedent, not with a three-stage test. Only a genuinely novel situation calls for incremental reasoning by analogy, using the Caparo factors. Omissions and harm caused by third parties are the main exception to liability for positive acts.
alt: Decision tree for whether a duty of care exists in negligence, following Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire Police and Caparo v Dickman.
description: Question 1: did the defendant's own positive act cause the harm? If no (an omission, or harm done by a third party), there is generally no duty unless the defendant created the danger, assumed responsibility, or had control of the third party or the source of danger (Smith v Littlewoods; N v Poole BC).
Question 2: is the situation genuinely novel, with no established category or precedent? If no, a duty exists: apply the established category, such as road users or doctor and patient (Robinson).
Question 3: by analogy with established categories, was the damage reasonably foreseeable, and was there sufficient proximity? If no, no duty.
Question 4: is it fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty? If no, no duty. If yes, a new duty is recognised incrementally (Caparo).

act.q: Did the defendant's own positive act cause the harm?
act.cite: Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire [2018] UKSC 4

omit.outcome: Omission or third party: generally no duty, unless the defendant created the danger, assumed responsibility or had control (Smith v Littlewoods; N v Poole BC)

novel.q: Is the situation genuinely novel, with no established category or precedent?

est.outcome: Duty exists: apply the established category (e.g. road users, doctor and patient)
est.cite: Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire [2018] UKSC 4

fp.q: By analogy: was the damage reasonably foreseeable, and was there sufficient proximity?

fjr.q: Is it fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty?

new.outcome: A new duty is recognised, developed incrementally
